name: Southeast Route / Standard
approach: Primary approach (White River side): From Hwy 2 at Coles Corner, follow Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (Forest Road 6400) to its end at the White River/Indian Creek Trailhead (~2,300 ft). Hike the White River Trail #1507 about 6 miles to the Thunder Creek crossing. A half mile past Thunder Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up an old, unmaintained sheep trail that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage through avalanche debris and brush to a lower basin (~4,175 ft), then steeply up to the upper Thunder Basin (~5,180 ft, roughly 6.5 miles and 2,880 ft of gain from the trailhead) — the standard high camp with a direct view of Tenpeak. Alternate approach (North Fork Sauk / west side): drive the Mountain Loop Highway to Forest Road 49 and the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,100 ft), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country via Boulder Pass and the Napeequa Valley to Tenpeak's north/northeast side — a much longer, more committing option (reported as ~31 miles and 13,500 ft of gain over 3 days for a full traverse) with 20+ stream crossings and dense brush. From the Thunder Basin camp, the route continues across talus and snow to a col east of the summit block (ice axe/crampons typically needed for the sometimes-firm snow), then climbs a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system, followed by a broken chimney/face pitch (Class 4 to easy Class 5 depending on conditions) to the summit; rock in the gully and chimney is loose, so helmet up and manage rope/party spacing to avoid dropping rock on others below.

approach_variants.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
approach_variants.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread up to about 5,000 ft. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The route carries three different elevations for that camp. Camp on the slabs by the tarns rather than at a number. A far longer alternative comes in from the west — North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
hazards: Loose, rotten rock in the summit gully and the broken chimney above it, directly over anyone belaying below
Dense slide alder choking the old sheep path to about 5,000 ft — the slowest half-mile of the approach by a wide margin
Crevasses on the small hanging glaciers crossed on the northern approach variations
Cornices and wind-loaded slopes on the approach ridgelines into early summer
White River Road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so the drive is the first thing to verify
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col east of the summit block is the base, and the thing that confirms it is the wind. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

Getting there is a single bearing from camp: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits east of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

The positive test for the start of the climbing: from the col the route takes a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

The second confirmation is a crack. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

What it is not: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

Rack and rock: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.

descent_text: Reverse the glacier and snow route to the basin.
pro_tips: Plan a multi-day trip given the long wilderness approach
Rope for the glacier and carry full crevasse-rescue gear

itinerary.cal: Best conditions are typically mid-summer once the approach brush has dried and snow on the col/gully has consolidated; check current avalanche/snow conditions on the SE col approach in early season.

days.note: Hike the White River Trail roughly 6 miles to Thunder Creek, then leave the maintained trail and follow the old, brushy sheep trail up the Thunder Creek drainage into the lower/upper basin. Route-finding through avalanche debris and brush makes this slower than the mileage suggests.
days.title: Approach to Thunder Basin high camp

schedule.label: Leave White River Trailhead
schedule.detail: Northwest Forest Pass required; trailhead at ~2,300 ft.

schedule.label: Leave trail at Thunder Creek
schedule.detail: Pick up the unmaintained sheep trail climbing the drainage.

schedule.label: Reach Thunder Basin
schedule.detail: Camp in the lower basin (~4,175 ft) or push to the upper basin (~5,180 ft) for a shorter summit day.

days.objective: Establish camp in Thunder Basin below the SE col

days.note: Alpine start up snow/talus to the col east of the summit block, then a loose gully and a broken, jam-crack chimney (class 4/easy 5th) to the top. Most parties rappel the chimney/face on descent rather than downclimbing since there are no fixed anchors — carry gear to build rap stations and leave slung horns/webbing.
days.title: Summit push via the SE col, gully and chimney

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start with ice axe and crampons for the snow slopes to the col.

schedule.label: Loose gully left of col
schedule.detail: ~85 ft of loose rock to a ledge.

schedule.label: Face pitch to broken chimney
schedule.detail: Class 4 / easy 5th class; good jam crack leads to the summit.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Typically a ~6-hour round trip from Thunder Basin.

schedule.label: Rappel/downclimb back to camp
schedule.detail: Build anchors on slung horns where no fixed gear exists; reverse gully and snow to Thunder Basin.

days.objective: Climb the Southeast Route to the summit and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach: descend Thunder Basin, rejoin the White River Trail at Thunder Creek, and hike the remaining 6 miles out to the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the White River Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day trip covering roughly 13 miles round trip and ~6,000 ft of net gain; the standard plan is one night in, a 6-hour summit round trip from Thunder Basin, and hike out the next day. Strong/fast parties occasionally compress it to a 2-day push, but the brushy unmaintained approach and loose, rappel-only summit pitch make the 3rd day worthwhile for most.

waypoints.name: White River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 6400; Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required, self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From Coles Corner on Highway 2, take Highway 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then follow White River Road (Forest Road 6400) to its end at the White River Trailhead, at about 2,300 feet. The road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so it's worth checking current conditions before you commit to the drive. At the trailhead, a Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required, and you self-issue a Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek crossing / Boulder Pass Trail junction
waypoints.note: White River Trail crosses Boulder Creek and passes the Boulder Pass Trail junction; well-traveled tread ends and maintenance gets sparser beyond here.
waypoints.directions: Hike White River Trail #1507 up the valley about 4 miles to the Boulder Creek crossing and the junction with the Boulder Creek Trail to Boulder Pass. Stay on the White River Trail.

waypoints.name: Old camp at Thunder Creek
waypoints.note: Established campsite next to the Thunder Creek crossing at the point where an old sheepherders' path leaves the White River Trail toward Thunder Basin.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the White River Trail about 2 more miles to the Thunder Creek crossing, where there is an established camp.

waypoints.name: Slide alder bushwhack
waypoints.note: Dense slide alder choking the old trail up to about 5,000 ft — the most difficult route-finding and bushwhacking on the approach.
waypoints.directions: Find the old, unmaintained sheep path that leaves the White River Trail near the Thunder Creek crossing and climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. It is hard to find, and the tread is choked with avalanche debris, blowdown and dense slide alder up to about 5,000 ft.

waypoints.name: Thunder Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Open basin with granite slabs and small tarns below Tenpeak's south side; standard high camp for the Southeast Route, with views of Glacier Peak and Clark Mountain.

waypoints.name: Notch/col east of the summit block
waypoints.note: Reached by crossing talus and a snowfield (crampons useful) from Thunder Basin; described by climbers as an 'incredibly windy notch' below the east face.

waypoints.name: Loose gully and broken chimney
waypoints.note: Southeast-trending gully with loose, wobbly rock leads to a ledge system, then a broken chimney with a jam crack (Class 4/low 5th) — watch for rockfall onto party below.
waypoints.directions: From the col, climb the loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Test every hold and keep the party out of each other's fall line.

waypoints.name: Tenpeak Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Tenpeak Mountain on the Chelan/Snohomish county line; reverse the chimney, gully, and col to descend.
waypoints.directions: From the ledge, climb the face to the broken chimney and follow its jam crack, Class 4 to easy Class 5, about 50 to 100 ft to the summit.
